title: The Eloquent Peasant
text:
A peasant named Khunanup loaded his donkeys with goods from his home in the Field of Salt and set off for Egypt's valley to trade them for food for his family. On the way he had to pass the estate of Nemtynakht, a man in the service of the high steward Rensi. Nemtynakht coveted the donkeys. He spread a cloth across the narrow public path so that the peasant had to steer his animals along the edge of a barley field. When one donkey snatched a mouthful of barley, Nemtynakht seized all the donkeys and beat their owner.

Khunanup took his case to Rensi himself. He spoke so beautifully that Rensi reported it to King Nebkaure, who was delighted. The king ordered Rensi to give no answer, so that the peasant would keep speaking and his words could be written down. In secret, the king had food sent to the peasant and to his wife and children.

Khunanup returned again and again, nine times in all, each time more desperate and more eloquent, reminding the steward that an official is meant to be a rudder for the helpless and a balance that does not tilt. After the ninth speech, Rensi had the petitions read to the king. The peasant's goods were restored, and Nemtynakht's property was given to him.
lesson: Officials owe a fair hearing to people with no power at all. And if you are the one being wronged, keep stating your case clearly and persistently, because persistence is sometimes what finally gets justice done.
people: Khunanup, the high steward Rensi, Nemtynakht, King Nebkaure
source: The Tale of the Eloquent Peasant, Middle Kingdom Egyptian text (Berlin papyri)
